cards.title: Introduction to OOP
cards.content:
What is Object-Oriented Programming?

Object-Oriented Programming (OOP) is a programming paradigm based on the concept of "objects", which can contain data (fields/attributes) and code (methods). Java is a class-based, object-oriented language designed to implement these principles.

OOP is structured around four primary pillars:

  • Encapsulation
  • Inheritance
  • Polymorphism
  • Abstraction

cards.title: Classes vs Objects
cards.content:
Classes and Objects in Java

A Class is a blueprint or template from which individual objects are created. It defines the state and behavior that objects of its type will have.

An Object is an instance of a class. It has a state (represented by fields) and behavior (represented by methods).

// Class Definition
public class Car {
    String color;
    void drive() {
        System.out.println("Car is moving");
    }
}

// Object Instantiation
Car myCar = new Car();

cards.title: Encapsulation
cards.content:
Encapsulation

Encapsulation is the mechanism of wrapping data (variables) and code (methods) together as a single unit. Under encapsulation, class variables are hidden from other classes and can only be accessed through public methods of their current class.

This is achieved by:

  • Declaring class variables as private.
  • Providing public getter and setter methods to modify and view the values.

cards.title: Inheritance
cards.content:
Inheritance

Inheritance is a mechanism wherein one class acquires the properties (fields) and behaviors (methods) of another. It facilitates code reusability.

We use the extends keyword to implement inheritance in Java.

class Vehicle {
    void start() { System.out.println("Vehicle started"); }
}

class Bike extends Vehicle {
    // Bike inherits start()
}

cards.title: Polymorphism
cards.content:
Polymorphism

Polymorphism allows objects to take on many forms. The most common use of polymorphism in OOP occurs when a parent class reference is used to refer to a child class object.

There are two types of polymorphism in Java:

  1. Compile-time Polymorphism (Static Binding): Achieved via Method Overloading (same method name, different signatures).
  2. Runtime Polymorphism (Dynamic Binding): Achieved via Method Overriding (same method signature redefined in subclass).

cards.title: Abstraction
cards.content:
Abstraction

Abstraction is the process of hiding internal implementation details and showing only functionality to the user.

In Java, abstraction is achieved in two ways:

  • Abstract Classes: Can have both abstract (without body) and concrete (with body) methods. Achieves 0 to 100% abstraction.
  • Interfaces: Used to achieve 100% abstraction (before Java 8 defaults). A class implements an interface using the implements keyword.
